articles.title: KEEPING THE UNITY OF THE SPIRIT
initials_text:
A B Brown, Linlithgow; A M Brown, Linlithgow; D A Brown, Bo’ness; D C Brown, Edinburgh; J T Brown, Edinburgh; R M Brown, Maidstone; R H Brown, Maidstone;
T R Campbell, Glasgow; M B Grant, Grangemouth; P A Gray, Linlithgow; N J Henry, Glasgow; N C McKay, Glasgow; W M Patterson, Glasgow; A S Pittman, Grangemouth; J S Speirs, Grangemouth

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: We have read a number of scriptures and it is not my intention that we go into them all in detail. The Lord will lead us as He wills. This verse in Ephesians, “using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace”, has been before me since I was asked to serve here. We read locally on Lord’s day the section in Ephesians 4: 1-16; that was not by chance. I would like us to enquire together what it would mean to use “diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace”.

Using diligence is an activity. It may not immediately be evident how the other scriptures bear on it, but I have read them as examples of persons who used “diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit”. If you read in 1 Samuel 25 you will find that Abigail went down four times in the space of two verses. In 2 Peter, Peter refers to the apostle Paul as “our beloved brother Paul”. Now Paul had withstood Peter to the face, but Peter says, “our beloved brother Paul”, and he says that God had given him wisdom. Peter said that Paul’s ministry was worth reading; so he used “diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit”.

Then we come to Philemon. Paul writes to Philemon after Philemon’s slave had run away and apparently stolen something that belonged to Philemon and Paul says, “I will repay it”. But when he asks Philemon to do something he also says, “knowing that thou wilt do even more than I say”. He gives his brother credit. And then finally we come to John. You may wonder what the connection is but you will remember that Peter denied the Lord three times, and it is John that tells us that he gave Peter access to the palace of the high priest. He acknowledges where we read that he was responsible for putting Peter in a place where he could fail.

So these are persons who are “using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit”; they are taking responsibility and showing respect and affection towards others. There is much teaching in this section in Ephesians. We may touch on it, but it is my exercise that we take this scripture up carefully and that we contemplate what the Lord would say to us in it. It would be good to get help together.

paragraphs.speaker: NJH
text: Even our own spirits are regulated in this divine arrangement, the unity of the Spirit; is that right?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: The injunction of scripture is, “be in subjection to the Father of spirits, and live”, Heb. 12: 9. One thing we can say about the Lord is that His spirit was never ruffled. He was angry when it was right to be angry, but His spirit was never ruffled. As He drew near to the cross, He was buffeted and spat upon but His spirit never changed.

paragraphs.speaker: NJH
text: The way it is put is “using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace”. It exists. I have got to be subject to it, and it involves our own spirits. Is that right?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I think unity of the Spirit involves what is formed in our affections. We see the uniting bond of peace, we see that the Lord “has broken down the middle wall of enclosure, having annulled the enmity in his flesh” - that was enmity between Jew and Gentile -“the law of commandments in ordinances, that he might form the two in himself into one new man, making peace; and might reconcile both in one body to God by the cross, having by it slain the enmity”, Eph 2: 14-16. The uniting bond of peace involves that everything that may have intruded on peace was dealt with at the cross; and the Lord bore that. So “the uniting bond of peace” would involve a recognition and appreciation of what Christ did on the cross.

paragraphs.speaker: WMP
text: If something is to be kept it must exist. Can you help us about that?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: What follows immediately is, “There is one body and one Spirit”. That is a fact in the sight of God. We are to arrive at “the unity of the faith”, but we are not said to arrive at the unity of the Spirit. Now the faith exists and it is one whole and it is complete, but our arriving at it may take a little time. But this suggests to me that as soon as a believer is baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Cor 12: 13), they have their place in the unity of the Spirit. And then it is a question of what is formed in me that would respond to that, but also what is formed in me that would desire to keep it. “Keep it” does not mean that I have to make it. I think keeping it involves keeping in the good of it. What would you say?

paragraphs.speaker: WMP
text: At the outset in Acts 2 where the Spirit came in it says, “they were all together in one place” v 1. I wondered if that showed how the matter of unity was there from the very outset. It is not something that had to be arrived at; it had been produced by the Lord’s own ministry to His own.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: “Together” is an important word in Ephesians. We are raised up together, and He has made us sit down together, chap 2: 6. And then we are “built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit”, chap 2: 22. God’s thought for us is that we should be together and that is why Christ is the Centre. He says in John 12: 32, “and I, if I be lifted up … will draw all to me”.

paragraphs.speaker: TRC
text: Following the Spirit coming in Acts 2, “they persevered in the teaching and fellowship of the apostles, in breaking of bread and prayers”, v 42. Would that have a bearing on what you are bringing before us?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I think so, and there is a moral order in that. The teaching and fellowship of the apostles really form the basis of our being together. You could not have the breaking of bread without the teaching and fellowship of the apostles, or at least not rightly, and you could not have prayers going heavenwards unless there had been a united appreciation of Christ. There would be individual prayers clearly, but you could hardly have collective prayer without an appreciation of Christ first.

paragraphs.speaker: RHB
text: How can this unity be breached?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I will be glad of your help. It simply cannot be breached, in the sense that it exists, but my appreciation of it might be diminished if I behave in a particular way, and I might also risk upsetting your appreciation of it. So, I do not think the unity of the Spirit can in itself be breached or broken, but using diligence to keep it would mean being together in matters and encouraging one another; it might involve a word of admonition. It is not simply all necessarily positive. There may be certain things to be dealt with but we would use diligence to do that with a view of preserving all in it, would you say?

paragraphs.speaker: RHB
text: I notice it is preceded in verse 2 by the exhortation to “bearing with one another in love”. We know from experience how, for example, personal feeling can arise and lead to irritation with one another. That interferes with the functioning of the body, does it not?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I think that is one of the reasons why the matter of witness is so important. The unity of the Spirit is maintained by keeping (if any matter does arise) to the facts of the matter. And it has been helpfully taught in ministry that one of the benefits of witness is that it restricts any matter to the issue that is extant, and does not bring in extraneous matters such as what a brother might have said many years ago in a completely different context. I think what you raise is very important for us to take account of. Really our focus needs to be on the Lord and on His rights in any situation, and if that is so then personal feeling would have to be set aside, would you say?

paragraphs.speaker: RHB
text: Yes, and the reference to one body is important, and it follows that verse, “There is one body”. That is the body of Christ, is it not, of which we are members? So the Spirit would help us to act as under Christ’s headship rather than in any way that may be marked by self-will, do you think?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Romans 12 teaches us how we find our place in the body and one of the first steps towards that is, “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the compassions of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice”, v 1. That is our intelligent service. But what we find in Romans 12 is that we are transformed according to the renewing of our mind, v 2. We are given the capacity to think differently and that includes the capacity to think differently about our brethren. In other words, to see them as God sees them. That helps us to find our place in the body and to recognise that each brother and sister has a place in the body. Further on in Ephesians 4, you get the fact that you are “renewed in the spirit of your mind”, v 4. Transformed according to the renewing of your mind is the capacity to think differently. “Renewed in the spirit of your mind” is that it has become characteristic. Believers who are using diligence to “keep the unity of the Spirit” are characteristically renewed in the spirit of their mind.

paragraphs.speaker: NCMcK
text: If I have the Holy Spirit, I have an obligation not to allow anything in me that would hinder my link with anyone else who has the Holy Spirit, to maintain that unity.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: That is important. Please say more to help us.

paragraphs.speaker: NCMcK
text: I wondered if it worked out practically in my own exercise to maintain things so that, if anyone else has the Spirit, there is nothing in me that would hinder them enjoying that unity with me. That would involve not only what I am when I fail in the flesh, but what I hold in regard to the truth, because that is largely what hinders Christians enjoying that unity, is it not?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Hence the unity of the faith is equally important. It is, “until we all arrive”. Everyone will be included in “the unity of the Spirit”, but some may not arrive at “the unity of the faith”. That is not God’s thought at all, and in a sense, whereas the unity of the Spirit is what is formed subjectively, “the unity of the faith” is what is taken account of objectively. And it never changes. We are told later on in Ephesians, “as the truth is in Jesus”, chap 4: 21. So we have it all in a Man. It is all there and it never has to alter. I think using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit is conducive to arriving at the unity of the faith.

paragraphs.speaker: NJH
text: When they were together at the beginning of the Acts “the unity of the faith” was present. They had gained from the ministry of Christ and then immediately the apostles came forward and set matters on, but “the unity of the Spirit” really involves our place in the body, does it not?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: It does, but the scripture says, “until we all arrive at the unity of the faith” and it does not say ‘and the knowledge of the Son of God’. It says, “until we all arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God”. So it is “the unity of the faith and the unity of the knowledge of the Son of God”. Thus we have the truth but we also have the One in whom the truth is exemplified, and there is nothing more conducive to unity than occupation with Christ. I think I can say that fairly because as Hymn 328 says,
Be Thou the object bright and fair
To fill and satisfy the heart;
If every heart is filled and satisfied with Christ that is conducive to unity.

paragraphs.speaker: DAB
text: Do you think what you are bringing before us flows from our enjoyment of our heavenly inheritance and portion? We have this coming in immediately after the three chapters of wonderful ministry from Paul to the Ephesians. What would you say as to that?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: What you say is important. There were nine and a half tribes that went into the land and two and a half did not. That was not God’s thought. It was not His thought that they should stop short of the fulness of the inheritance. We have been reading Ephesians locally and looking particularly at the blessings that are available in it. One thing that has struck me in our enquiries together is the range of the blessings that God has in mind for His own. First of all they are immeasurable, they are never going to be exhausted, and secondly, they are so far superior to anything that the world could offer, that the world really fades out of sight. And if we enjoy that we would be using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in view of everyone enjoying it, and in view of God having His portion.

paragraphs.speaker: DAB
text: I think the basis of that is love, is it not? Bearing with one another in love. So do you think that the whole matter really flows from the enjoyment of our spiritual inheritance, our spiritual portion. It is not the other way around. We do not work up to this, do we? This should flow really, should it not? I was thinking of the Lord’s word in John. Twice He refers to the commandment “that ye love one another”, chap 15: 12, 17. And from that do you think the working out of these things should take place in a very straightforward manner.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Yes. It is interesting, is it not, that it is described as “A new commandment … that ye love one another”? The reason it is new is because of what the Lord says, “as I have loved you”, John 13: 34. They had seen love exemplified, personified in a way that they had never seen it before. And that was now the standard. That is a very uplifting thing. You may say that is very testing, perhaps it is to me, but nevertheless it puts love at the standard at which God sees it.

paragraphs.speaker: AMB
text: The first verse of the chapter refers to “the calling wherewith ye have been called”, and the need to walk worthy of it, and everything really flows from that, does it not? What you have drawn attention to in verse 3 is in the same sentence. I wondered if we might get some help on “the calling wherewith ye have been called”? We have been called. It is God’s calling, is it not, and it is a heavenly calling? In 1 Corinthians it is linked to “the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord”, chap 1: 9. Would you say something for our help as to it?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Say more to help us. What does it mean to have a heavenly calling? What would that be?

paragraphs.speaker: AMB
text: It links to what we have just been speaking about as to the heavenly portion of the saints. Jews were accustomed to an earthly portion, and they fell short of it and were disappointed. The believer is called into the fellowship of God’s Son which has to be worked out here on the earth in our walk together and in testimony, but what is in view is being with Christ forever. What we work out here in our lives and in our testimony is to be consistent with that, is it not, as looking on to it? It should become apparent that believers’ lives, and their hearts and minds, are linked up with Christ in heaven.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Paul refers to it as “the prize of the calling on high of God in Christ Jesus”, Phil3: 14. It was something that he thought was valuable and worth striving for. There was no doubt about the calling, but Paul wanted to be in the good of that; he pursued. Ephesians 4 is not addressed to individuals, although it is up to us to work it out individually, but it is good to remember that not only do I have a heavenly calling, so do you. We are going to enjoy that heavenly calling together eternally; so it causes us to regard each other on the footing that God regards us.

paragraphs.speaker: AMB
text: Does it also bring in the thought of dignity? The heavenly calling, “the calling wherewith ye have been called”. Well, who has called us? It is God that has called us, is it not? So it is a dignified matter. In Corinthians it is associated with the fellowship of God’s Son. We are part of something that is very great and very dignified and the centre of it is Jesus Christ, God’s Son.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Paul had quite a lot to correct in Corinth but he opens his first epistle by addressing them as “called saints”, chap 1: 2. That means they were saints by divine calling. So in that sense he said to the brethren, ‘I am going to remind you of what you are in the sight of God’. That is a very valuable and positive thing to do for one another. Keep in our minds what the saints are in the sight of God.

paragraphs.speaker: WMP
text: That is really what Abigail did. She maintained David at the height of what he should be.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Yes, exactly. And she said, “Upon me, my lord, let the iniquity be”. She did not pretend there was no iniquity. She did not say, ‘It does not matter’. But she said, ‘Let it be on me. I will do what is needed to put this matter right’. Keeping the unity of the Spirit is not about pretending that something has not happened. That is what the world does; it brushes things over. But the Lord “might reconcile both in one body to God by the cross, having by it slain the enmity”, Eph 2: 16. God did not act as though nothing really happened. God said, ‘Something has happened, and now it must be dealt with in righteousness’, and that is how unity will come about. The enmity will be slain.

paragraphs.speaker: JSS
text: Does the fact that it is a bond of peace confirm what you are saying? There can be no peace without righteousness. There is a bond of peace. Can you say something about that?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I am glad you bring that in. I have been thinking about that scripture, “righteousness and peace have kissed each other”, Ps 85: 10. In the world sometimes you can have peace without righteousness, but that is not so in God’s eyes. It is not peace by compromise. The uniting bond of peace is that we recognise that everything that is required to be dealt with in righteousness was dealt with at the cross. So, John says to those to whom he writes in his first epistle, “if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin”, chap 1: 7. Why does it add that, as to the blood? The thought is that “we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another”, but John as it were adds, that if there is a difficulty with that, here is the solution. John generally approaches things from a different standpoint from Paul. He approaches things differently, but they have the same end in view. Having fellowship with one another, and using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit, would not be too far apart from one another, would they? Help us more.

paragraphs.speaker: JSS
text: Conditions of peace are important, are they not? You might say peace is something that we enjoy, but it is really important that there are conditions of peace amongst believers that there might be what can be enjoyed as to the presence of the Lord and the praise of God and so on. It is more than just what we have to enjoy, do you think?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: We have spoken about the work that the Lord has done to bring about peace, but it is also said in the prophet that “This man shall be Peace”, Mic 5: 5. What appeals to me is that God rests in Christ, and so can we. And I do think what you say about conditions of peace is important. That is when food can be enjoyed. You find in the history of king David that there was a time when he put garrisons in certain cities, 2 Sam 8. In that sense, having established peace he would then maintain it. What has been said about self-judgment is important. The first place there has to be a garrison is in me. I have to make sure I am not doing something that would disrupt the peace. But in a general sense God wants the peace to be enjoyed so that He can enjoy His portion.

paragraphs.speaker: JTB
text: There is a very affecting reference in Zechariah: “the counsel of peace shall be between them both”, chap 6: 13. Does it bring out that peace is divinely established?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I think that. I think what you say is most helpful, and you will be familiar with the fact that it is in Zechariah also that it says, “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, even against the man that is my fellow” 13:7. How could God have peace? He would have it in righteousness. We think of the Lord’s sacrifice but consider what a sacrifice God made, do you think, in order that there might be a righteous peace?

paragraphs.speaker: JTB
text: Yes, Zechariah is helpful. He says, he “shall sit and rule upon his throne” (chap 6: 13), but then it adds, “he shall be a priest upon his throne”. So we can rely on the priestly service of Christ in securing and working towards these peaceable conditions, can we?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Yes, indeed, and how thankful we are that He is “a merciful and faithful high priest”, Heb 2: 17. And the order matters. You cannot do without either. It is not that we say we will just have mercy and not faithfulness - that will not do at all - but the mercy comes first.

paragraphs.speaker: ABB
text: You mentioned Abigail going down. What would you say as to that?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Well, I have often been struck by it. Firstly, “she hasted”. “She hasted” and then, “she lighted off the ass”. So that is the first going down. And she “fell before David on her face”, so that is the second. “Bowed herself to the ground”, that is the third. And, “fell at his feet”, that is the fourth. So she hasted, and she went down and then she said, “Upon me, my lord, upon me let the iniquity be”. I think “using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit” would involve that. If there is something that needs to be resolved, I want to make a very clear distinction between being hasty and hastening. There is nothing helpful about being hasty, but when there is an opportunity to put something right we should hasten to take it. So in Numbers 16 the plague had to come, and in verse 46-47, “Moses said to Aaron, Take the censer, and put fire thereon from off the altar, and lay on incense, and carry it quickly to the assembly, and make atonement for them; for there is wrath gone out from Jehovah: the plague is begun. And Aaron took as Moses had said, and ran into the midst of the congregation”. I do not suppose they had seen the high priest running before. But they saw it that day: he ran. Now, persons lost their lives and that was the just judgment of God in that dispensation. But when Aaron had the opportunity to bring in God’s mercy, he ran to do it. He did not stand on the margins of the camp and say that these people brought it on themselves: he ran. He laid aside his own dignity and went towards where he could best provide the help. I think that is what Abigail did, and she brought provisions with her. She had something to offer.

paragraphs.speaker: ABB
text: That is fine. I was just thinking about the word ‘diligent’. It implies care, and I think that marks discretion, marks our actions too. David refers to that; so that is another matter, do you think? There are things that we can do quickly, right things, but care should always mark our actions, do you feel?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I am glad you have drawn attention to it. If we want to help in any situation the question would be, what provision can I bring? I can easily say what I think is wrong. That might be true even, but what provision can I bring? She brought provisions with her. So I think what you are saying is helping to open up the thought I had in mind. Using diligence might involve being able to provide something.

paragraphs.speaker: RMB
text: One of the primary things that seems to have marked Abigail was her concern for David, was it not, that there should be no stain upon him against that day when he would be anointed king publicly? I was just thinking about that in connection with your exercise and how it might apply to us today. Would it help us to be together if the honour of the Lord, the honour that is due to His precious name, was our chief concern? We could encourage one another in that way.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I do think that. I have thought of Matthew 18 in relation to the part dealing with assembly discipline; it is concerned with the Lord’s rights. It is not concerned with my rights. If someone sins against me I have to forgive him seventy times seven: that is what the Lord says to Peter. But when the Lord’s rights are at stake then careful steps are taken, and at each step the thought is that there should be a righteous resolution. But, if there is not, then there is the moment when the matter must be told to the assembly. And even then, that is in view of a righteous resolution in that the person may listen, but if they do not listen then a further step is taken. So, that would bear on what was said about being careful. These steps are taken carefully but they cannot be evaded, because then that would not be recognising what is due to the Lord.

paragraphs.speaker: RMB
text: So it tests our spirituality, does it not, when matters come up? There are often a number of things which the brethren have to think about and pray about. There may be a brother or a sister that is a particular matter of concern, or maybe a question of carrying the confidence of the saints and respect for the assembly, but does Abigail show us that the chief thing is what is due to the Lord? You and I might not see eye to eye on a matter but if we can keep that before us it will help us to arrive at a common judgment, do you think?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I do think so. And just to be simple about it, if you and I do not see eye to eye on a matter I should be quite inclined to think that you will have been exercised about it, and that you are not just simply saying this because you happen to think that way. So I would want to give a brother or a sister credit if they had a concern about something, even though I might not quite see it that way. What would then help us is if we were both exercised about the same thing, which is the Lord’s rights, then He will help us to come to a point where they are properly recognised.

paragraphs.speaker: RMB
text: I remember Mr Walkinshaw saying that true unity amongst the saints is brought about by subjection to the same Lord in the power of the same Holy Spirit.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: That is a very good way to put it. I am thankful you have said that, as it in a way sums up what I have in mind by way of an exercise.

paragraphs.speaker: MBG
text: I was thinking about what has been said in Galatians 6: 1: “Brethren, if even a man be taken in some fault, ye who are spiritual restore such a one”; and the note to restore is ‘mending’. I wondered if that might relate to the care and diligence that we have been speaking about. It says, “such a one in a spirit of meekness”. You were speaking about Abigail going down four times. You really see a spirit of lowliness and meekness there, do you not? And the outcome is that a situation that could have had a negative outcome did not have a negative outcome. I just wondered if that might be something we should consider. We have spoken about being tested as to our spirituality, and that verse in Galatians brings together the thought of “ye who are spiritual” and this moral feature of meekness.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I just speak very simply; I know how much mercy the Lord has shown to me; and therefore, I think it behoves me to be meek in relation to anything that I might need to take up with anyone else. It does not absolve me of the responsibility to do it, but it certainly affects how I would go about it. I think the link between that scripture that you have quoted, “if even a man be taken in some fault, ye who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of meekness” is really consistent with this “using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit”. That man has been taken in a fault; we want him back into the enjoyment of the unity of the Spirit. Restoring, or mending, means that things are put right in a way that is righteous, because a person is not mended if it is not done righteously. The mending involves that what needs to be done is done, and the Lord’s rights are honoured in how the matter is approached. It is interesting, it says in Zechariah 10: 6, “And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will bring them back again; for I will have mercy upon them”, and this is the point I want to underline, “and they shall be as though I had not cast them off”. God says he would put them right back to where they were, as though all this history, all this failure, had not happened. “For I am Jehovah their God, and I will answer them”. Well, God has answered in Christ, and thus He can say, “they shall be as though I had not cast them off”.

paragraphs.speaker: MBG
text: In relation to what you have said, you see an example of that with Paul with Eutychus. He went down, but he brought Eutychus right back up again to the full enjoyment of the height of what they were enjoying in that room at that time. I wondered if that was an example. And Paul, also, describes himself as the first of sinners (1 Tim 1: 15) and “less than the least of all saints”, Eph 3: 8.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Yes, he did. One feature of Paul’s activities towards Eutychus was that he said, “his life is in him” Acts 20: 10. And again just to your point, “ye who are spiritual”. A spiritual person would discern life where it is and seek to recover it to the height that God had in mind.

paragraphs.speaker: ASP
text: That is helpful. I wondered if we can have an example as to what Abigail says. “Upon me, my lord, upon me let the iniquity be”. I suppose we see it in what Paul says to Philemon. I wondered if you could help as to how we take that on ourselves.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Judah says to Joseph in Genesis 44, when Joseph said he would detain Benjamin, “And now, let thy servant stay, I pray thee, instead of the lad a bondman to my lord, and let the lad go up with his brethren”, v 33. So Judah said he was willing to take responsibility for this matter. It is very easy to say that somebody else did something wrong and it is not my problem, and that is not Christianity. The Lord never said that something was somebody else’s problem: “who himself bore our sins in his body on the tree”, 1 Pet 2: 24. Now of course, if I steal money, for example, and that is exposed, then it was not you that stole it and it is not your fault it was stolen either; but, the question is, what is then to be done about the matter that might safely restore a brother? So the first thing is we take responsibility for the restoration, but secondly, if a brother or sister with whom I am local does something that they should not have done, the first question I need to ask myself is, did I set them a right example? And was there more I could have done in order to help them? So, Abigail admitted to David that he was denied provision by Nabal that he was righteously asking for. David was perfectly righteous to ask for Nabal to provide for him; so she says, ‘I will bring the provision instead, but do not go to battle with this man. Do not go to war’. That was in view of the protection of David in the time that he would become king. So I go back to this, if a situation arises saying, “upon me let the iniquity be”, is basically saying, what provision can I bring, in righteousness, that will help to resolve this?

paragraphs.speaker: ASP
text: I think that is helpful. It must take some spiritual wisdom to do that. I feel very tested in it.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: So do I. What is in my mind, and in my affections too, is that the enemy would love to disrupt what we have. Therefore, it behoves us under the Lord’s headship to do what we can to protect what He has given us, and to protect one another. That is my exercise.

paragraphs.speaker: DCB
text: I have been thinking about spiritual influence. There is a positive spiritual influence with Abigail. Where you read about John he was for once not bringing to bear spiritual influence on Peter. So we have to be very careful, do we not, and conscious that what we do has influence?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Yes. John thought that what he was doing was helpful and it was very unhelpful. He brought Peter into a place where Peter could fail. It could be said that it was kind of John to let him in. Well, no, it was not. We have been taught and it bears repeating, that the right motive for doing something is no excuse for a wrong action. It is the action that counts, not the motive. So, we may have a right, but the question is, what is due to the Lord? So, I think what you say about having a right spiritual influence is important. And the other thing is, if somebody in a position of responsibility does something it has a much bigger impact than somebody doing it when they are young. Now it does not make it right when you are young and wrong when you are old, but what I mean is those of us who are responsible: I have to accept my responsibility for the example I set, because it will be noticed. And that again is using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace.

paragraphs.speaker: NJH
text: John as the writer discloses who it was that got Peter in; it was himself. That was a right move.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: That is what I meant about the fact that John came to it that he had to accept that he should not have done what he did. In that sense it could be said, Peter would be with the Lord by the time John wrote this. You say, what difference does it make? John says, ‘No I have to put this right’. I have to say, I had my part in this, and I think that was a righteous move.

RB The parallel has been made to Abigail and her acting in all lowliness and meekness, but I was just thinking of all the examples that you have touched on in the subsequent verses to Ephesians 4 to demonstrate that, and also these other matters that were mentioned, “long-suffering, bearing with one another in love”; that was referred to at the outset. Could you help us more as to what that involves? Bearing with one another. You have talked about what is hasty, but bearing with one another I think is the key to this as was stated, is it not?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: We could refer to the way that Mr James Taylor carried teaching he had heard as a young man for many years before bringing it before the brethren when he felt they were ready to receive it. That is an example of bearing with one another in love. And the remark made earlier helps us too. A brother might see something a little differently from me. Well, what am I going to do? Am I going to pray about it? I may seek to speak in grace to the brother, but I will also bear with it. When it reaches a point of any refusal to accept the Lord’s rights in a matter, that in a sense draws a line. If there is outright refusal to accept what is due to the Lord then the Lord would indicate that, and we might have to take a further step. What would you think?

paragraphs.speaker: TRC
text: In that sense, if I think differently to another brother it should be a burden and a concern to me, should it not? The answer is having the Lord before us and His rights.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Exactly that. And it is not about whether I am better at persuading you, or you are better at persuading me. What you said is most important. What would the Lord have in this matter? Not what do I think, or what would I like, or what I might prefer. What would the Lord have in this matter? And if our minds are set on that, then in that sense the Lord becomes our object, as He is, and that helps us towards resolution.

paragraphs.speaker: RMB
text: Abigail is also a type of the assembly, is she not, as faithfully caring for His interests? And that is what we desire should mark each of our local assemblies, do you think?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: I like the reference at the end of Proverbs, as to the woman of worth, and it says, “The heart of her husband confideth in her”, Prov. 31: 11. Well, that means he has confidence in her. I know it means he shares things, but it also means he has confidence in her. You would not confide in someone in whom you had no confidence. The Lord has had confidence in His assembly. Well, it is my responsibility to see that that confidence is justified.

paragraphs.speaker: RMB
text: I was thinking of that when you alluded earlier to Matthew 18 and the Lord says, “tell it to the assembly”, v 17. That implies that the Lord Jesus is looking to the assembly to act for Him to do things in the way that He would do it, and to maintain all that is due to His holy Name, do you think?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Yes, and it is good for us to remember what precedes that part of Matthew 18. First of all at the end of Matthew 17, the spirit of sonship is brought in: “Then are the sons free”, v 26. So any matter that is to be taken up is to be taken up in the spirit of sonship. And what precedes that is the Lord transfigured before them, v 2. So, the assembly is the place where the Lord’s rights, as ascended, are valued and held. But then when you go through Matthew 18 there are three individuals referred to. There is a little child, and a lost sheep, and a brother. It is possible for someone to be all three. They are not separate persons necessarily. And all I mean is that as we come towards that point where something may have to be raised with someone, then let us take account of what they are. They may be a little child; they may need some care and instruction. They may be a lost sheep; perhaps they have wandered off, but they are always a brother. That much is definitely the case. So, we take it up in the light of Christ glorified in the light of sonship and in the light of what the person is to God and then we ask, how do the Lord’s rights stand in this matter?.

paragraphs.speaker: DAB
text: You have used the term ‘the Lord’s rights’. Help us as to what they are.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: They are supreme in the first place. So there are not greater or higher rights in that sense. I speak of the Lord now both as Man but also as God. His rights are supreme. He has a right as Creator: He made us. He has the right as Redeemer: He bought us. He has a right over believers as their Head, but in order to come into the good of His headship we must first acknowledge His rights over us as Lord. In other words we must be subject to Him in the kingdom before we come into the full good of the assembly. He has a right, too, to our affections. That is why Paul says in 1 Corinthians 11, “the Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was delivered up, took bread”, v 23. The Lord in that sense told Paul that, at the darkest hour, He set on the Supper which would allow us to remember Him. So He has a right to our affections both individually and collectively. We could extend the list but there is no sphere in my life in which the Lord does not have supreme rights over me. Christ is the Head of every man, and the woman’s head is the man. Christ’s Head is God. That is the order that God has put in place in order that Christ’s rights might be recognised, and God will see to it that they are. “Wherefore also God highly exalted him, and granted him a name, that which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of heavenly and earthly and infernal beings, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord to God the Father’s glory”, Phil 2: 9-11. God will see to it that His rights are acknowledged.

paragraphs.speaker: DAB
text: The Holy Spirit within us would enable us to appreciate and to value these rights.

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: He would, because He would always promote the rights of Christ in our affections, which, I feel, is so important. The hymn says -
If He claims our hearts’ affections
Unreserved as His own (Hymn 111).

paragraphs.speaker: NJH
text: The Spirit lifts a banner when the enemy comes in like a flood, Isa 59: 19. That is a rallying point, is it not?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Yes. One of the banners was Jehovah-nissi, ‘Jehovah my banner’, Exod 17: 15. The loved one in the Song of Songs says, “his banner over me is love”, chap 2: 4. The Lord is that central gathering point. You remember in Numbers where the tribes camped they were each by the standard of his father’s house. They were identifiably of that house. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. That was their banner; they were identified as such. And we have an opportunity to be identified with the Lord publicly every Lord’s day morning when we assemble to break bread.

paragraphs.speaker: RHB
text: In relation to the breaking of bread, is the exhortation to prove ourselves and thus eat related to using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: That is an interesting connection, and a helpful one. If I am proving myself then I am removing, in that sense dealing with, judging, what may intrude on the enjoyment of the unity of the Spirit, for me and for others. I do feel this, the importance of being careful not only that I keep myself in the enjoyment of the unity of the Spirit, but that I do not disturb it for others either. I have a responsibility in relation to that too, do you think?

paragraphs.speaker: RHB
text: The Supper is the greatest expression of our fellowship and bond together, and the very fact that that is before us should sharpen our sensibilities as to that matter, should it not?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Well, it is as simple as this. If I go to the Supper locally I want every brother and sister to be comfortable to sit down with me. I want us all to be occupied with the Lord, not with what someone has said or done, but with the Lord and what He has done. And therefore I would be using diligence to ensure that that is so. And we get a drawing together of the unity of the Spirit and the unity of the faith in the expression in verse 15, “holding the truth in love”. That really brings together the unity of the faith and the unity of the Spirit: “holding the truth in love”. You do not have one without the other. But that “we may grow up to him in all things, who is the head, the Christ”. And really, the Supper, one might say, is the evidence that we are holding the truth in love and that we are growing up to Him. He is our Object.

paragraphs.speaker: NCMcK
text: It was immensely important that Peter, John and Paul should maintain this, not just for their own enjoyment or for their own reputation but in view of the import to the testimony that nothing should be discredited of the immense truth which they imparted. And that this should be seen that this was workable, that the unity of the Spirit was workable, because we are left with the record that the apostles maintained that, are we not?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: We are. I think that is a very helpful way to put it. So Peter would see to it that there was no stain on his relationship with Paul. John would see to it that there was no stain on his relationship with Peter. And Paul would ask a brother to do something - and this was a responsible brother, because he says, “to the assembly which is in thine house”. And, as was helpfully asked earlier, what does it mean to say, “upon me let the iniquity be”? Well, Paul said as to Onesimus, ‘I will help pay his debt. I will pay his debt. I could do that righteously and I will do it’. But he said, ‘I am asking you, Philemon, to do something, and I am asking you in the knowledge that you will do even more than I ask you’. Well, that is a very fine way to speak to a brother, not speaking to them doubtfully or uncertainly but saying, ‘I have confidence in this brother that whatever I ask him to do he will not just do it but he will do better’.

paragraphs.speaker: NJH
text: The relationship of “beloved brother” means the relationships were greatly improved, is that right?

paragraphs.speaker: PAG
text: Well, exactly. “And Ananias answered, Lord, I have heard from many concerning this man” - Saul of Tarsus - “how much evil he has done to thy saints at Jerusalem; and here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon thy name”, Acts 9: 13, 14. That is to the end of verse 14. Three verses later, “And Ananias went and entered into the house; and laying his hands upon him he said, Saul, brother, the Lord has sent me”, v 17. He spoke to the Lord; he told the Lord about his concerns, and, putting it simply, the Lord said, ‘Ananias, I have dealt with all of these concerns. Now you can have a relationship with this man as a brother’. That is what the Lord does for us. We speak about using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit, but it is in the uniting bond of peace. If there is a difficulty the Lord will have dealt with it. He is able to do that.

paragraphs.text: In John’s gospel, the Lord expresses His desire for His disciples, but also for “those who believe on me through their word” - which includes every believer, “that they may be all one”. In this address my exercise is to speak about what the Lord Himself did so that His desire “that they may be all one” should be fulfilled.

Much of Isaiah’s prophecy relates to Israel and to the nations around it, but we can apply it at the present time. If the Lord’s own were to be “all one”, there was a cost that had to be paid. I want to occupy us, as I am able, with the Person of Christ, but also with His work, and all that it secures. I could have read Psalm 22, which also speaks very touchingly of the way the Lord went, touching on the forsaking and all He suffered, His death, His resurrection, and what He brings to God; but I chose this section because we might think of Psalm 22 as having the character of the burnt-offering, which is the ground of atonement and the ground of our acceptance. It is what is for God, what God took particular pleasure in, but in this section I have read in Isaiah we also get what Jesus did for us. I would like that to lay hold upon us. As I get older, I recognise more the value of what Jesus did for me. I must recognise that the value was first for God; that is the supreme matter. But then I come to the value of what He did for me, and that the way He took in order to do that was the way of suffering.

God could have commanded that His own should be all one. It says as to the creation, “he spoke, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast”, Ps 33: 9. But for all the glory and wonder of creation, that would not have made known the heart of God as the way of sacrifice and suffering did, and God wanted us to know His heart. He wanted us to know that He was willing to pay a measureless price so that His heart of love might be revealed to us in all its fulness and glory, to the end that we might know and recognise that there is a God supreme in the universe, none greater, who so desired to make Himself known to us and to claim us for His own, that He would give His own Son to die for us, and to shed His precious blood and to be buried and then, glorious message, to rise again the third day. “Why seek ye the living one among the dead? He is not here, but is risen”, Luke 24: 5, 6.

I can offer you nothing greater than to be occupied with the Man of God’s choice, the Man of all His counsels, the One of whom He said prophetically, speaking of David as he was to be anointed king, “I have found David … a man after my heart, who shall do all my will”, Acts 13: 22. What did the will of God cost Jesus? Well, He will come in in His glory: “Behold, my servant shall deal prudently; he shall be exalted and be lifted up, and be very high”, and so He will. His name is “King of kings, and Lord of lords”, Rev 19: 16. In order for that exaltation and for Him to have that “garment dipped in blood” (v 13) “many were astonished at” Him - “his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the children of men”. It says in Isaiah 50: 6, “I gave my back to smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair; I hid not my face from shame and spitting”. Think of that! - the Lord of glory, the Creator of the universe, the One “by whom also he [God] made the worlds” (Heb 1: 2), the One who is “the effulgence of his [God’s] glory and the expression of his substance” (Heb 1: 3), coming into manhood and not hiding His “face from shame and spitting”. And, as we read later on in chapter 53, He “made intercession for the transgressors”. He interceded for those very persons who so abused Him.
Now, there is a hymn which is credited to the same writer as, ‘Jesus! the very thought of Thee’, that says -
Thy head once full of bruises,
So full of pain and scorn,
’Mid other sore abuses,
Mocked with a crown of thorn;
Thy Head once bowed and wounded
On the accursèd tree
Is now, O Lord, surrounded
In highest majesty.

That was written in what we call the Reformation. The writer had light in his soul. The head that is now ‘surrounded with highest majesty’ is the head that was wounded with a crown of thorn, and struck: “Prophesy, who is it that struck thee” (Luke 22: 64) - all this in order that God’s will might be done and in order that there might be an answer to the heart of God. He accepted it all from His God and Father. He could say, “My Father, if it be possible let this cup pass from me; but not as I will, but as thou wilt”, Matt 26: 39. He accepted it because it was His Father’s will. The Lord’s words in John 12 often affect me, “Now is my soul troubled, and what shall I say?”, v 27. Think of that! Human expression was insufficient to describe the depth of His feelings as He faced the cross. “What shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But on account of this have I come to this hour. Father, glorify thy name. There came therefore a voice out of heaven, I both have glorified and will glorify it again”, v 27, 28.

Think of how God was glorified in Jesus coming into manhood, growing up “before him as a tender sapling, and as a root out of dry ground: he hath no form nor lordliness, and when we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him”. This was Israel’s judgment of him, and so would mine be apart from the work of new birth by the Holy Spirit. Apart from God’s gift of repentance and faith, that would be my attitude too, and yet God saw to it that it was not so. Think of the Lord saying, “My Father worketh hitherto and I work” (John 5: 17). He worked in order that we might be saved, in order that we might come to it that this One who grew up entirely dependent on God, as Man, is the One who had come to save us, “despised and left alone of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief”. Beloved brethren, it may be that here today there are persons who are sorrowing and acquainted with grief, and maybe we do not know anything about it, but there is a “man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief” who knows your heart, who has come near to bless. “For such a high priest became us, holy, harmless, undefiled, separated from sinners, and become higher than the heavens”, (Heb 7: 26), and He went this way of grief and sorrow in order that we may have His present sympathy. Such a Man is the One whom God would have glorified in our hearts.

“One from whom men hide their faces; - despised, and we esteemed him not”. Perhaps you have had to face “the reproach of the Christ”, Heb 11: 26. Persons would hide their faces from you, want nothing to do with what you do, despise and hold you to be of no esteem, accusing you of believing foolish thoughts and holding to ideas that you cannot prove. I can see the proof as I look at those gathered here of the power of God, and “I am not ashamed of the glad tidings; for it is God’s power to salvation”, Rom 1: 16. I can see it, and everyone who has faith can see it, but the Lord knows what it is to be despised and not to be esteemed by persons who turn away from you because they believe what you do is foolish. He understands it and He sympathises for He has faced the same Himself.

“Surely he hath borne our griefs and carried our sorrows”. When Isaiah is quoted in Matthew it says, “Himself took our infirmities and bore our diseases”, chap 8: 17. Believers bear infirmities and diseases. The Lord bore them in His spirit. We have been rightly taught that what He bore in His spirit, He took away in His power. He Himself was never marked by infirmity or disease. He was perfect, but He bore them in His spirit. Think of a time when He met one suffering, it says of Him that “he groaned “, Mark 7: 34. He felt it deeply that one should be under the scourge of disease as a result of sin, but He bore it in His spirit.

“And we, we did regard him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted”. Beloved, if you or I had been “stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted”, we would not have endured for one instant. Those who mocked thought, as they stood around the cross, that all that He had said was now being set at nought. Indeed, they said, “He trusted upon God; let him save him now if he will have him”, Matt 27: 43. They regarded Him “stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted” and they found it an object of mockery.

But then the writer goes on to explain that His suffering was not in order that man should mock Him, but rather that God’s rights should be upheld. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and with his stripes we are healed”. He went that way for you and for me. He went that way to remove everything that stood between man and His God and He went that way to remove everything that stood between believer and believer. Everything contrary is taken away at the cross, and the blessing comes in the acknowledgement made in verse 6: “All we like sheep have gone astray”. If I think that the only person that has gone astray is someone else, then I am not right. I have gone astray and I confess it, but I also know that the cost of that was borne by Jesus. “All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way” - who of us has not been self-willed? - “and Jehovah hath laid upon him the iniquity of us all” - “of us all”: there is nobody missed out there. All who trust Him will find that that their iniquity was “laid upon him”. And He went after the straying sheep; we see it in Luke 15. He goes after it until He finds it and then He brings it back. He brings it back to where it should have been. There is no recorded rebuke for the sheep that had gone astray. “He lays it upon his own shoulders, rejoicing”, Luke 15: 5. How far did He go? He went to the cross and to the grave and then He came out in triumph and in glory.

I say one other thing in relation to the Lord’s prayer, “that they may be all one”. We are sometimes told, rightly, that you can put your name in Isaiah 53: 5 so you could say, ‘But he was wounded for my transgressions, he was bruised for my iniquities; the chastisement of my peace was upon him, and with his stripes I am healed’. Well, I can say that. Can you? But I ask you another question: “that they may be all one”, can you look round every time you are gathered with your brethren and put every other brother and sister’s name in there? I do not say that as doubting it. Maybe you have a doubt about a brother or a sister. Can you say that He was wounded for their transgressions? Of course you can. One of the things that occupation with Christ does is to cause us to look on one another as those who were sufficiently valuable for Christ to die for them, even “the weak one, the brother for whose sake Christ died”, 1 Cor 8: 11. I would be careful not to exclude myself from saying that I have been a weak brother too. It is not just somebody else. “Jehovah hath laid upon him the iniquity of us all”.e was wounded for their transgressions.

“He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, but he opened not his mouth”. We spoke earlier about the Lord’s rights in the assembly, and that is the place where they are held and honoured and upheld, but the Lord never stood up for His own rights when here as Man. “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, but he opened not his mouth”. This is the Man who could have called on twelve legions of angels (Matt 26: 53) to set Him free. One angel was sufficient to slay a hundred and eighty-five thousand in one night (2 King 19: 35); so twelve legions would be a powerful force, “but he opened not his mouth”. Instead “he was led as a lamb to the slaughter, and was as a sheep dumb before her shearers, and he opened not his mouth”. And even when matters were put to Him, He simply says, “Thou sayest”, Matt 27: 11. He made no defence of Himself. He accepted it all from His Father. And He went on. “He was taken from oppression and from judgment; and who shall declare his generation?” None could. The centurion recognised something. He says, “Truly this man was Son of God”, Matt 27: 54. But none can “declare his generation” for “no one knows the Son but the Father”, Matt 11: 27. That is how great a Person He is, and yet, such a One came into manhood and went that way.

“He was cut off out of the land of the living”. Think of how He felt about it! “Take me not away in the midst of my days”, Ps 102: 24. He was about thirty-three years old. The Lord of glory was taken by wicked hands when He was but a relatively young Man in the midst of His days, and not only sentenced to death but crucified. Peter says, ”ye, by the hand of lawless men, have crucified and slain” (Acts 2: 23) for things He had not done. He was crucified for what I did, not for what He did. “He was cut off out of the land of the living; for the transgression of my people was he stricken”. Think of the grace of God in that! Israel, whom He had come to call, shunned and rejected Him. Through the parable they say, “We will not that this man should reign over us”, Luke 19: 14. Directly when asked, they say, “Take him away, take him away, crucify him”, John 19: 15. They say, “Not this man, but Barabbas. Now Barabbas was a robber”, John 18: 40. That is who they chose, and yet “for the transgression of my people was he stricken”. He was stricken for those who hated Him and who saw to it that He would be hanged on a cross. What a Saviour!

“And men appointed his grave with the wicked”. They came to break His legs in order that they might cast Him into a common grave, but they found that He was already dead, and that the blood and the water came out as a result of the action of a soldier with a spear piercing His side; and righteous men came, and He was not put in a grave with the wicked. “He was with the rich in his death”. It says, “neither wilt thou allow thy Holy One to see corruption”, Ps 16: 10. And, of course, no corruption affected His body, but God went further, we might say, in protecting what was precious to Him. He was put in “a new tomb in which no one had ever been laid”, John 19: 41. There was no corruption even in the area in which He was placed. God so valued what was there and He reached out and claimed Him, “raised up from among the dead by the glory of the Father”, Rom 6: 4. How great a Saviour!

“Because he had done no violence, neither was their guile in his mouth. Yet it pleased Jehovah to bruise him; he hath subjected him to suffering”. It is not altogether straightforward to understand “it pleased Jehovah to bruise him”. I think what it relates to is what scripture speaks of as “the good pleasure of his will”, Eph 1: 5. “Yet it pleased Jehovah to bruise him”: it was right that it should be so in order that God might demonstrate, through a way of suffering, the greatness of the love that was towards us. “When thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin”: it is interesting that that is the trespass-offering that is referred to there. The sin-offering, I think, relates to the holiness of God, but the trespass-offering is more directly associated with the Person offended. It is a fine thing to come to it that sin is, of course, an afront to the holiness of God and to His rights, but it is an affront to Him personally. The younger son recognised that. He got as far as saying, “I have sinned against heaven and before thee”, Luke 15: 21. He recognised who had been affronted by the sin he had committed and yet, “thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin”. I cannot go into it now, but follow up the trespass-offering. It covers the holy things of Jehovah, the commandments of Jehovah and our relationship with our neighbour. These are the three things it covers. That is what is drawn out here.

“He shall see a seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Jehovah shall prosper in his hand”. We read at the end of John 3 that “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things to be in his hand” (v 35), and what He has given into the hand of Christ will prosper not just for time but eternally. “He shall see of the fruit of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied”. He got a foretaste of that in the garden with Mary. “Jesus says to her, Mary. She, turning round, says to him in Hebrew, Rabboni”, John 20: 16. There is just a touch there of the assembly in whom He could confide, but the first thing He says is, “go to my brethren and say to them, I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”, John 20: 17. He was going to see “the fruit of the travail of his soul”; He was going to see His brethren. Think of that: “and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant instruct many in righteousness; and he shall bear their iniquities”. Instruction in righteousness may mean that we become conscious of something that is not right. “He shall bear their iniquities”. There is a means to deal with it, whatever it is.

“Therefore will I assign him a portion with the great”. We spoke earlier about, “a name, that which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow”, Phil 2: 9, 10. “He shall divide the spoil with the strong: because he hath poured out his soul unto death”. I would like you to think of that matter of pouring out, “poured out his soul unto death”. When He speaks of His blood the Lord says: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you”, Luke 22: 20. And then the gift of the Spirit: “and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which ye behold and hear”, Acts 2: 33. This dispensation of grace was inaugurated by divine Persons pouring out. How wonderful it is to take account of that. Whatever is needed, divine Persons have poured out. “Because he hath poured out his soul unto death, and was reckoned with the transgressors” - that was me - “and he bore the sin of many”. Why does it not say all? Because you have to trust Him to get the benefit, and if you have not trusted Him before now, this is the time to do it; “behold, now is the well-accepted time; behold, now the day of salvation”, 2 Cor 6: 2.

“And made intercession for the transgressors”: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do”, Luke 23: 34. And that intercession was successful because these persons for whom He had interceded came in, in the early Acts. When Peter preached to them, they said, “What shall we do, brethren?”, Acts 2: 37. They were convicted in their souls that what they had done was wrong. “And having heard it they were pricked in heart, and said to Peter and the other apostles, What shall we do, brethren? And Peter said to them, Repent, and be baptised, each one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ, for remission of sins, and ye will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit”, Acts 2: 37, 38. What a God we have! Those persons who caused that Christ should be put on the cross, who were responsible for it, “were pricked in heart” (v 37), and did Peter say that what they had done was too awful to be forgiven? No, he said what he would say to everyone, “Repent, and be baptised, each one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ, for remission of sins, and ye will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit”. That was the cost that we might be reconciled to God. That was the cost that we might be one.
May the Lord bless it for His Name’s sake.

Who can set forth the love of God? Who can tell the blessedness which lies enfolded in the words, “God is love”? When men are in question, and man’s state in view, it is said that “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all”, 1 John 1: 5. Man’s estrangement from God has not affected Him so as to make Him other than He is; and for man there is no light as to anything until he knows God. No true judgment can be formed; things cannot be seen in their relation to each other, until God Himself is known.

But when the light reaches us, and we learn what God is, what is He? Our portion of Scripture answers - “Love”. This is what He is, absolutely; the nature of His Being. This gives us the spring of all His activity in respect to His own, shows what must be the wondrous character of it, and tells of its end. He acts according to that which He is, in the sovereign supremacy of love which is above all the power of evil; love dictates the style and manner of His activity; and the end is His own satisfaction when He will rest in His love.

There are many who think of kindness or benevolence as love. Our own ways may instruct us in the difference. Benevolence relieves a beggar at your door, or leads you to care for the poor in their dwellings; the child who is nurtured in the bosom of your family knows your love. So is it said, “The Lord is good to all; and his tender mercies are over all his works”, Ps 145: 9. This has ever been so from creation onwards, and many touching instances we may all have known. On the other hand it is said, “Hereby perceive we the love of God because he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3: 16); and “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us”, Rom 5: 5. The love is shown to us by that which is altogether outside our earthly circumstances, and the knowledge and enjoyment of it we have alone by the Holy Spirit. As the sun’s rays reach us and gladden us outwardly in this world, so by the Holy Ghost God’s love reaches and gladdens our hearts, but its proper sphere is heavenly.

So the apostle goes on to speak of the manifestation of God’s love as regards ourselves. It was His intention that we, delivered from all that held and oppressed us, should be placed before Him, able to enjoy His love and to respond to it. With this in view He sent His only begotten Son into the world. From the lips of the Lord Himself we have the first mention of this love and its purpose in John 3. Having spoken of the necessity for the uplifting of the Son of man, as meeting before God the whole question of man’s state as ruined and under the judgment of God, He then adds, “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life”. He thus shows that it is the love of God that led to the question of man’s state being fully met by means altogether apart from his own works and thoughts, and this with the definite end in view that the believer should have eternal life. Thus does divine love come forth, and become active in the sphere of our sin and ruin, meeting all that was involved, but to the end that we may be brought into its own sphere, and have its full enjoyment there. Eternal life is the knowledge of the Father, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, His sent One.

The only-begotten Son is He who is naturally (as it may be said) the object of divine affections, and the One by whom they are perfectly known. By Him, then, has God’s love been declared, for no other could declare it. He has become Son of man for the accomplishment of its purpose. He has become the propitiation for our sins, and as the uplifted One has glorified God about the whole matter of sin. He has lifted from us the pressure of judgment and set us perfectly free. Now by the Spirit He gives us to participate in His state as the One risen from the dead, and brings us in association with Himself, into the enjoyment of the divine affections which are so perfectly known to Himself.

As risen from the dead He said to Mary, “go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father, and to my God, and your God”. When He stood in the midst of His disciples He breathed into them, and said, “Receive ye the Holy Ghost”, John 20: 17, 22. This is the action of the last Adam, who is a quickening spirit. As the Lord God had breathed into the nostrils of the first Adam and he became a living soul, so now, the last Adam forms His company in living association with Himself by breathing into them, and the gift of the Holy Spirit as forming their state in accordance with His own. In speaking of them as His brethren, He looks upon them in the light of the full purpose of God’s love, and according to that which He constitutes them in virtue of His death for them. They are the many grains which are the result of the death of the one Corn of Wheat. To them, as such, He can unfold all the depths of that “blest name of love“ - “my Father”.

It is said, “Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment; because as he is, so are we in this world”, 1 John 4: 17 margin. If God acts in His own love He cannot stop short of His own satisfaction. His satisfaction is seen alone in that blessed, risen Man who is before Him. The love of God is perfected with us in that as He is so are we in this world. It brings us into a relationship with God, into favour and divine affections, of which the pattern could alone be found in that blessed One. Judgment will come upon all that is outside the circle of God’s satisfaction, but for that day we have boldness, for divine love has set us in that circle according to its own thought and intention. What blessed confidence does this give! “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear”, v 18.

We are made painfully conscious that the world as it now is; is not the circle of divine affections, but rather that of the hatred and hatefulness of man. Yet love has been manifested, and as we receive the truth of it we are drawn by it into its own circle of heavenly joys, of which we have the present apprehension and enjoyment by the Holy Ghost, and in company with the Lord Jesus, the Son of God. As we have this wondrous enjoyment, a responsive affection is formed; we love Him, because He first loved us. and we are able to love one another. We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.
May the God, whose love it is, grant to us each its unclouded enjoyment!
Notes
Scripture quotations are from the King James’ Version.

This article was first published in a volume entitled Comfort. A two-volume collection of all his published ministry, entitled Ministry by Joseph Revell, is available from www.lulu.com. Our brother lived from 1851 to 1900, and died unexpectedly in Winnipeg.

articles.title: A SONG FOR THE "FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK"
articles.author: Joseph Pellatt

paragraphs.text: Thy love, blest Lord, in death made known,
Has touched our hearts anew;
Responsive love delights to own,
All praise to Thee is due.
The loaf declares us to be one,
The flesh no more is seen;
The Spirit's unity we own,
Where diverse we had been.
"The cup of blessing which we bless",
Speaks loud of love divine;
Love flowing out in righteousness,
Where God's bright glories shine.
Thy death announced, we wait that day
When Thou wilt surely come;
The sceptre of God's kingdom sway,
And we with Thee at home.
While thus we call Thee, Lord, to mind,
Thou dost in Spirit come,
With us Thy brethren here to find
Thy love's attractive home.
The Father's Name Thou hast declared,
His love is there well known;
While with Thee all that love is shared,
Thyself, Thy brethren, one.
There Thy blest voice delights to raise
In tones of deepest joy,
The hymn of holy, heavenly praise,
In bliss without alloy.
